title: Volume Booster: 7 Proven Steps for Fast and Smooth Valves
text:
Control Valves

 Volume Booster: 7 Proven Steps for Fast and Smooth Valves

 A large actuator can take many seconds to fill when only the positioner supplies the air, which is too slow for surge, trip and pressure control duties. A volume booster copies the positioner signal and adds plenty of air flow, so the valve strokes fast yet still positions accurately.

 
 1:1 Pneumatic Relay 
 Bypass Needle Tuning 
 Stroking Speed 
 Fail Action 
 




 Large control valves often move too slowly because the positioner relay cannot pass enough air. A correctly installed and tuned volume booster solves that problem without making the loop unstable.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a pneumatic volume booster works, how to install and tune it with a positioner and how to estimate the faster stroking time it gives.


 
 
 

 What Is a Volume Booster?


 A volume booster is a pneumatic relay with a fixed 1:1 ratio that takes the small output signal of a valve positioner and reproduces the same pressure at the actuator, while drawing a much larger air flow straight from the supply line. It sits between the valve positioner and the actuator and makes big valves stroke many times faster.


 A positioner relay has small internal passages, so it is designed for accuracy, not for flow. On a large diaphragm or piston actuator with tens of litres of volume, that small flow means stroking times of 20 seconds or more.


 
 
 Image credit: ControlAir . Product photo courtesy of ControlAir, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 The volume booster does not change the control signal, it only adds air capacity. The positioner still decides the final valve position, and the booster just helps the actuator get there quickly.


 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 Inside the Booster: How the Relay Works


 Inside the body there are two diaphragms, a supply valve and an exhaust valve held on a common stem. The signal pressure from the positioner acts on the top diaphragm and the output pressure acts on the bottom one.


 
 Signal Rises Positioner output increases above the booster output

 Supply Opens Diaphragm pushes the stem and opens the supply port

 Actuator Fills High flow supply air fills the actuator quickly

 Balance Output equals signal and both ports close

 Signal Falls Exhaust port opens and actuator air vents fast




 When the signal is higher than the output, the force imbalance opens the supply port, and air rushes into the actuator. When the signal falls, the exhaust port opens and dumps actuator air to atmosphere through a large vent.


 Do You Know?
 Most boosters have a small deliberate deadband, so tiny signal changes do not open the main ports at all. Emerson states a nominal deadband of 2 to 5 percent of positioner output span for the Fisher 2625, depending on the exhaust port size.



 The Bypass Needle Valve and Why It Matters


 Every good volume booster has an adjustable bypass restriction, usually a needle screw, between the signal port and the output port. It works like a small needle valve that lets the positioner feed the actuator directly for small changes.


 For small steps, the positioner air passes through the bypass and the booster ports stay closed, so positioning stays smooth and precise. For large steps, the pressure difference across the bypass grows until the volume booster opens fully and delivers its high flow.


 If the bypass is closed too far, even small changes force the booster to act, and the valve overshoots and hunts. If it is open too far, the pressure difference never builds up and the booster hardly helps.


 Quick Tip
 Start with the needle about four turns open from fully closed, as the Fisher 2625 manual suggests, then close it gradually during step tests. Stop when large steps are fast and small steps still settle without overshoot.



 7 Steps to Install and Tune a Volume Booster


 
 1
 Check Need
 Confirm the required stroking time is not met by the positioner alone.


 2
 Size Air Supply
 Use a high capacity filter regulator and at least 1/2 inch supply tubing.


 3
 Common Supply
 Feed the positioner and booster from the same regulated supply.


 4
 Pipe Correctly
 Positioner output to booster signal port, booster output to actuator.


 5
 Seal Joints
 Use thread sealant paste, not tape, on pneumatic connections.


 6
 Set Bypass
 Open the needle about four turns, then tune on step tests.


 7
 Verify
 Run small and large steps, record stroking time and overshoot.





 Use the same regulator for the positioner and the volume booster, because a different supply pressure upsets the balance and can lock the valve in one position. Clean and dry air is essential, as explained in water vapour in instrument air lines .


 Moisture and oil that freeze or stick inside a booster cause sluggish or erratic movement. Keep the instrument air dew point well below the lowest ambient temperature at site.


 Stroking Time and Air Volume Formula


 A quick estimate of stroking time compares the free air needed to fill the actuator with the flow the pneumatic path can deliver. Free air is the actuator volume multiplied by the absolute pressure ratio.


 
 Free air needed: Vfree = V × (P + 1.013) ÷ 1.013 
 Fill time: t = Vfree ÷ Q × 60 

V in litres, P in bar gauge, Q in normal litres per minute, t in seconds

Example:
V = 20 L, P = 4 bar g
Vfree = 20 × 5.013 ÷ 1.013 = 98.97 L
With booster, Q = 1500 Nl/min: t = 98.97 ÷ 1500 × 60 = 3.96 s
 Without booster, Q = 150 Nl/min: t = 39.59 s 



 This is a rough average flow method, because real flow falls as the actuator pressure approaches supply pressure. Treat the result as a guide for selection, and confirm the actual time in a stroke test.
